t: Digit Operations to Make Two Integers Equal
o: Transform n into m by ±1 on individual digits, never passing through a prime (including the start). The cost is the sum of all values n takes, starting value included. This is a shortest-path problem on the graph of same-digit-count non-prime integers, where moving from u to a neighbor v costs v; Dijkstra with initial distance dist[n] = n gives the minimum total. Primes up to 9999 come from a sieve. If n or m is prime, return −1.
k: States are non-prime integers with the same digit count as n; edges connect numbers differing by 1 in one digit (leading digit can't become 0, preserving digit count).
Accumulated cost = sum of visited node values, so Dijkstra with dist[start] = n and edge weight = destination value solves it.
Primality is checked with a precomputed sieve up to 9999; a prime n or m immediately means −1.

a.i: Each state expansion tries ±1 on every digit, filters to valid non-prime same-width numbers, and relaxes with cost + neighbor value. The first time m is popped, its distance is optimal.
s: If n or m is composite-check-failing (prime), return -1
Dijkstra from n with dist[n]=n; neighbors are digit ±1 variants within [10^(d-1), 10^d−1] and non-prime; return dist when m pops
a.t: O(P log P · d) where P ≈ 9000 reachable states and d ≤ 4 digits — effectively instantaneous
a.sp: O(P) for distances and the sieve

w: Modeling as shortest path is the entire difficulty; the cost definition (including the starting value) maps cleanly onto dist[start] = n. Pitfalls: forgetting that the STARTING number must be non-prime (example 3), forgetting m must be non-prime, and letting the leading digit hit 0 (changes digit count). Reachability can genuinely fail (example 2: 4 is boxed in by primes 3, 5 and single-digit primes), hence the −1. Follow-up: reconstruct the actual cheapest sequence by storing parent pointers.
